query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloys, the accelerated coupled degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature is driven by a synergistic interplay at the phase boundaries. Mechanical wear preferentially removes or damages the protective passivating film on the more corrosion‐prone phase (typically the softer fcc phase in a lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure), thereby exposing fresh reactive interfaces that set up micro-galvanic cells between the phases. This, in turn, accelerates localized corrosion, which weakens the interphase bonding and further enhances wear, establishing a vicious cycle of degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar microstructure (e.g., alternating soft fcc and hard B2 phases) that possesses an initially intact, passivating surface oxide layer typical of high-temperature environments.
generation.intervention: Expose the material to simultaneous mechanical wear (sliding contact) and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature, compared against control conditions with isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., around 700°C or higher where passivation is marginal), in a corrosive environment (e.g., presence of aggressive ions) under sliding wear conditions that mechanically disrupt the surface film.
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase boundaries between the soft fcc phase and the hard B2 phase, where the mechanical disruption leads to exposure of chemically distinct regions predisposed to galvanic coupling.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically breaches the passive oxide layer, particularly at vulnerable phase boundaries, exposing the softer phase to aggressive corrosion. The exposed interfaces then act as sites for micro-galvanic corrosion, which not only accelerates the chemical attack on the material but also degrades the mechanical cohesion between phases, further amplifying the wear process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline tested under isolated wear or corrosion, the total degradation (combined material loss) will be significantly higher under coupled conditions. Individually, both the measured wear rate and the corrosion rate will be elevated due to the feedback loop, with the degradation being more than just the additive effect of the two isolated phenomena.
generation.baseline: A matched sample tested under only wear or only corrosion at the same temperature and environmental conditions, or an alloy with a similar composition but a homogenized (single-phase) microstructure that does not support extensive galvanic coupling.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds under conditions where: (a) elevated temperature compromises the stability of the passivating film, (b) the corrosive medium provides sufficient ionic species to drive galvanic reactions, and (c) the applied mechanical load is enough to continuously disrupt the surface film; outside these ranges, the synergy may not be significant.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of the mechanical disruption versus the chemical weakening at the phase boundaries are not precisely quantified, and exact thresholds (temperature, sliding load, corrosion aggressiveness) for the onset of the synergistic degradation have yet to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the eutectic high-entropy alloy with its intrinsic lamellar microstructure, and (2) a control alloy with either a single-phase microstructure or one in which the phase boundaries are modified (e.g., via heat treatment) to minimize galvanic coupling. Subject both to identical testing conditions involving simultaneous sliding wear in a corrosive environment at elevated temperature. Monitor both the total material loss and the spatial distribution of damage (using microscopy) over time.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate using profilometry or mass loss measurements
Corrosion rate via electrochemical techniques or weight loss due to corrosion
Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM) to assess damage at phase boundaries
Surface chemical composition analysis (e.g., XPS) to detect passivating film integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the eutectic alloy does not exhibit a significantly higher combined degradation rate (i.e., the sum of wear and corrosion damage is not synergistically greater) than the control alloy, and if microstructural examination fails to reveal obvious damage at the phase boundaries indicative of galvanic interaction, then the hypothesis that mechanically induced exposure of reactive phase boundaries drives the accelerated degradation will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
